title: Tenant-aware Kernel Ladder: Architecture, Profiling, and Runbook
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Summary:
This handbook documents the tenant-aware kernel ladder: a runtime subsystem that adaptively promotes and demotes kernel configurations per-tenant to meet latency SLOs while optimizing GPU utilization and cost. It combines architecture rationale, kernel scheduling rules, profiling playbook, benchmarking plan, rollout checklist, and an incident runbook.

Purpose and scope:
- Audience: serving runtime engineers, SREs, on-call, and performance engineers.
- Scope: design and operational procedure for the kernel ladder (promotion/demotion, telemetry signals, safety guards, and rollback).
- Non-goals: hardware provisioning, global autoscaler policies, and model architecture changes.

1) High-level design
Overview:
- Kernel ladder is a discrete set of kernel profiles (K0..K4) that trade throughput/cost for worst-case latency. Each profile is a precompiled kernel bundle + scheduler hints (batch slice size, preemption score, qcache warmup).
- Per-tenant control plane maps tenant -> ladder policy. Policy attributes: base_profile, min_profile, max_profile, promotion_cooldown_s, demotion_cooldown_s, telemetry_weights.
- Runtime components:
  - Ladder controller (per-node): watches incoming telemetry and per-tenant session state, emits profile-change intents.
  - Kernel activation agent (per-GPU): applies profile bundles and issues kernel handshake; ensures safe rollback if activation fails.
  - Quota crediter: ensures profile changes respect slot accounting and kernel credits.
  - Telemetry exporter: publishes promotion/demotion events and rationale to metrics and traces.

Architecture diagram (text):
- Request -> Request-classifier -> Tenant policy lookup -> Ladder controller -> Kernel activation agent -> GPU dispatcher -> Kernel execution -> Telemetry sink

2) Policy model and scheduling rules
Policy fields (table):
| field | type | description | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| base_profile | string | default kernel profile for tenant | K1 |
| min_profile | string | lower bound allowed | K0 |
| max_profile | string | upper bound allowed | K3 |
| promotion_metric | string | telemetry metric used for upshift | tail_latency_99ms |
| promotion_threshold | string | threshold to trigger promotion | 150ms |
| demotion_metric | string | metric used for downshift | avg_tokens_per_second |
| promotion_cooldown_s | int | min seconds between promotions | 60 |
| demotion_cooldown_s | int | min seconds between demotions | 300 |

Scheduling rules (short):
- Prefer non-disruptive profile changes: when possible, move only new allocations to the higher profile and let existing sessions finish (soft promotion).
- Hard promotion: if tail latency > promotion_threshold for 3 consecutive 1-min windows, force immediate kernel swap for hot sessions with warm-up prefetch.
- Demotion: only demote when sustained over a 10-minute window and GPU utilization headroom > 25%.
- Safety: at most 20% of a node's kernels can be in an experimental (K4) profile concurrently.

3) Telemetry & SLOs
Canonical metrics (exported to metrics namespace rwd.runtime.ladder):
- tenant.tail_latency_99_ms (gauge, ms)
- tenant.avg_latency_ms (gauge, ms)
- tenant.token_throughput_tps (gauge)
- node.gpu_utilization_pct (gauge)
- ladder.promotion_events_total (counter)
- ladder.failed_activations_total (counter)

SLO guidance (example tenant class):
- Enterprise interactive: p99 latency <= 180ms for requests <= 256 tokens, availability >= 99.95%.
- Standard API customers: p99 latency <= 300ms, availability >= 99.9%.
- Background batch: p99 latency <= 2s, availability >= 99.5%.

Alert thresholds (examples):
- Pager (SEV2): tenant.tail_latency_99_ms > 250ms sustained for 5m AND ladder.promotion_events_total increased by > 30% in 10m.
- Ops (SEV3): ladder.failed_activations_total > 5 in 10m on a single node.

4) Profiling playbook (how to collect targeted signals)
Objective: gather representative traces and microprofiles to decide ladder step definitions and promotion thresholds.
Steps:
1. Identify representative tenants: choose 3 tenants per SLA class (interactive, standard, batch).
2. Use sampled tracing at 1% of requests for 24h with request context "ladder-prof"; capture kernel dispatch timings, batch shapes, KV cache hit ratio, and prefetch latencies.
3. Run microbenchmarks on candidate kernel bundles: run 10k synthetic short requests (32–64 tokens) and long requests (512 tokens) across K0..K4. Collect p50/p95/p99 and memory working set.
4. Create a ladder-definition artifact (YAML) for each tenant class. Example: 

---
tenant_class: interactive
ladder_steps:
  - id: K0
    description: minimal-latency (low-batch, high-priority, small kernels)
    expected_p99_ms: 120
    cost_factor: 1.8
  - id: K1
    description: balanced
    expected_p99_ms: 160
    cost_factor: 1.0
  - id: K2
    description: throughput-optimized
    expected_p99_ms: 260
    cost_factor: 0.6
---

5. Validate ladder offline using the workload replay harness in benchmarking suite (see section 5).

5) Benchmarking plan and acceptance criteria
- Bench harness: use the operational-workload-simulator with recorded traces. For each ladder candidate, measure: node throughput, tail latency, GPU idling, kernel switching time, and cost-per-token estimate.
- Acceptance criteria (release gating):
  - p99 latency improvement for promoted tenants >= 25% vs base_profile under matched load, AND
  - Cost uplift per-token <= 40% for interactive tenants (for enterprise customers with higher SLOs), OR
  - No more than 5% increase in node-level tail latency for mixed-tenant workloads.

6) Release & rollout checklist
Pre-flight:
- Generate ladder YAML artifacts and commit to repo rwd/ladder-defs.
- Run full bench harness and attach results to release ticket.
- Code review and canary gate: enable ladder in canary region with traffic fraction 0.5% for 2 hours.
Gradual rollout:
1. 0.5% traffic - 2h - check metrics and failed_activations_total.
2. 2% traffic - 4h - validate p99 and GPU utilization headroom.
3. 10% traffic - 6h - watch cross-tenant tail latencies.
4. 50% traffic - 24h - if stable, escalate to 100%.
Rollback criteria (automated):
- Any single-node ladder.failed_activations_total > 10 in 5m -> immediate rollback of ladder on that node.
- Cross-tenant node p99 latency regressions > 15% sustained for 15m -> rollback to previous kernel bundle set.

7) Operational runbook (on-call playbook for SEV2/SEV3)
When triggered: detect via alert or manual observation.
A. Initial triage (first 10 minutes):
1. Check ladder.failed_activations_total and node.gpu_utilization_pct graphs.
2. Identify affected tenants and node(s) via trace ids and metrics.
3. If failed_activations_total spikes on a node: ssh to node and inspect /var/log/rwd/kernel-activation.log for handshake errors; run `rwdctl kernel status --node $NODE`.

B. Mitigation steps (10-30 minutes):
1. Soft demote affected tenant(s): `rwdctl ladder set --tenant $TID --profile K1 --mode soft`.
2. If kernel activation handshake fails repeatedly, drain node from scheduler and trigger a rolling restart of kernel agent: `rwdctl node cordon $NODE && rwdctl agent restart kernel-agent --node $NODE`.
3. If cross-tenant p99 regressions: temporarily enable global conservative policy: `rwdctl ladder set-global --max_profile K1` (admin only).

C. Post-incident actions (30m+):
1. Collect the following artifacts and attach to incident ticket: kernel-activation.log, last 30m of ladder telemetry, sample traces (ladder-prof), bench-run summary.
2. Open a performance regression ticket if ladder caused regressions, assign to kernel-scheduling team.

8) Known limitations and issues
- Kernel activation latency: some legacy kernels require a cold handshake that can take 120–250ms. Workaround: prefer soft promotions and warm-prefetch for affected models.
- Cache-skew edge-case: per-tenant promotions may create KV cache fragmentation; mitigation: periodic KV compaction job (daily) and prefetch heuristics.
- Rollout oscillation: naive promotion/demotion based solely on p99 can oscillate. The ladder uses cooldown windows and hysteresis, but complex multi-tenant bursts may still cause flapping. Future fix: add predictive smoothing using short-term AR models.

Known issues table (brief):
| id | symptom | workaround | owner |
| KLD-101 | failed kernel handshake on A100p 2.0 nodes | cordon node and restart kernel-agent | kernel-scheduling team |
| KLD-112 | tenant p99 spike after hard promotion | revert tenant to previous profile and soft-warm | SRE/perf |
| KLD-117 | KV cache fragmentation for >1000 active tenants | run kv-compact and limit concurrent promotions | runtime-infra |

9) Postmortem and metrics to track after rollout
- Reduction in tenant-tail-p99 per SLA class
- ladder.promotion_events_total/k (normalized) vs failed_activations_total
- Node-level avg GPU-ptime (time kernels are active) and idle fraction
- Cost per token estimates before/after ladder

10) Ownership, contacts and escalation
- Primary maintainers: kernel-scheduling (team alias: team-kernel-sched@redwood.com)
- On-call rotation: kernel-scheduling SRE and runtime-platform SRE (see oncall roster link: /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-roster)
- Pager escalation: SEV2 -> oncall SRE, then engineering manager.

References and artifacts:
- rwd/ladder-defs repository (internal)
- Benchmark runs: /artifacts/bench/ladders/2026-01 (links attached to release ticket)
- Related pages: predictive-slotting-and-quota-orchestration-2026, delta-routing-and-cost-partitioning-architecture-2026

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets
- Check a tenant's current profile:
  rwdctl ladder get --tenant $TID
- Force soft promotion for debugging:
  rwdctl ladder set --tenant $TID --profile K2 --mode soft --reason "debug/latency-test"
- Dump last activation logs for node:
  sudo journalctl -u rwd-kernel-activation -n 500 | tee ~/activation-tail.log
